text: An adversarial example is an input that's been deliberately, carefully changed just enough to make a model misclassify it, while a human looking at the same input either doesn't notice anything different or doesn't think the difference matters. There's no malformed data here, no broken schema, nothing a validator would catch. The vulnerability lives in the model's decision boundary itself, and that's exactly what this lesson unpacks.

The textbook demonstration is a photo of a panda that a trained classifier labels correctly, with high confidence. Add a layer of noise to every pixel — small enough that the image still looks like the same panda to you — and feed it back in. The same classifier now calls it a gibbon, just as confidently. Nothing meaningful changed about the picture. What changed was a nudge computed from the model's own math.

That nudge has a name: the Fast Gradient Sign Method. An attacker with access to the model's internals computes the gradient of its loss with respect to the input — essentially, which direction makes the model more wrong, fastest — and then shifts every input dimension a tiny, fixed amount in that direction. A budget, epsilon, caps how large that shift is allowed to be, which is what keeps the result imperceptible instead of just a different input.

Three terms carry through the rest of this chapter. The perturbation budget bounds how big a change counts as adversarial rather than simply a different input. White-box access means the attacker can see the model's gradients directly; black-box means they only get to submit inputs and watch outputs. And transferability is the uncomfortable finding that an attack built against one model frequently fools a completely different model trained on the same kind of task.

That transferability result matters because it means hiding a model's internals isn't a real defense on its own. Next lesson takes this same mechanism out of the image-classifier lab and into the systems a security team actually has to defend — malware classifiers and spam filters that researchers have published real, peer-reviewed techniques for evading.
